content_title: New Tick-Borne Virus Discovered in China Traced to Hundreds of Fever Cases
content: An Asian longhorned tick in July 2025. (Griffin Dill/University of Maine via AP) Chinese researchers, working with U.S. collaborators, have identified a previously unknown tick-borne virus that appears to be responsible for hundreds of previously unexplained fever cases in China. The new pathogen, named Asian longhorned tick nairovirus (ALTNV), belongs to the genus Orthonairovirus in the Nairoviridae family. The findings were published in The New England Journal of Medicine on Sept. 2. The University of Minnesota’s Center for Infectious Disease Research and Policy (CIDRAP) also reported on the discovery. ALTNV infection is associated with a flu-like illness marked by fever, fatigue, gastrointestinal symptoms, and abnormal laboratory results. The researchers also found evidence that co-infection with ALTNV and Dabie bandavirus (DBV) can lead to more serious illness. How Virus Was Found The discovery began with a medical mystery. In some parts of China, more than 30 percent of patients with symptoms resembling severe fever with thrombocytopenia syndrome (SFTS) test negative for DBV, the virus known to cause the disease. SFTS is a tick-borne illness that can cause high fever and dangerously low platelet counts. Its reported case-fatality rate is between 10 and 30 percent. The unexplained cases suggested that another pathogen might be circulating. Researchers collected samples from patients with fever and a history of tick exposure at sentinel hospitals in areas of China where tick-borne diseases are common. They used RNA sequencing and virus-isolation techniques to identify the pathogen. Genetic analysis placed ALTNV in the Orthonairovirus genus. Its amino acid sequence was less than 80.04 percent identical to those of other known species in the genus, supporting its classification as a distinct virus. The researchers tested 3,163 patients with fever and a history of tick exposure. Overall, 10.4 percent tested positive for ALTNV based on detection of viral RNA or antibodies. Among patients who had tested negative for DBV, 15.1 percent were positive for ALTNV. Patients infected only with ALTNV generally developed an influenza-like illness. Fatigue was reported in 84 percent of patients, gastrointestinal symptoms in 80 percent, low platelet counts in 38 percent, and elevated liver enzymes in 36 percent. All patients with ALTNV alone recovered without lasting complications. The picture was different among patients infected with both viruses. Of 38 patients with ALTNV and DBV coinfection, seven—18.4 percent—died. Coinfected patients also had higher rates of respiratory symptoms and impaired kidney function than patients infected with DBV alone. The Tick Behind the Virus The researchers also tested 47,428 ticks collected in 15 Chinese provinces. ALTNV RNA was detected in 1.29 percent of them, with the highest detection rate found in Haemaphysalis longicornis, commonly known as the Asian longhorned tick, at 1.75 percent. Laboratory experiments showed that H. longicornis can transmit ALTNV to mice. Infected mice developed tissue changes and produced antibodies against the virus. The findings provide evidence that ALTNV is a newly discovered emerging tick-borne virus associated with human illness. The researchers said the fact that ALTNV and DBV circulate in the same areas and share the same tick vector highlights the need for better testing to distinguish between the two infections. Chinese Military Scientists Included The study was led by seven researchers from Beijing's State Key Laboratory of Pathogen and Biosecurity, which is under the administration of Academy of Military Medical Sciences (AMMS). Two other authors are listed as directly affiliated with the AMMS, China's top-level military research institution. U.S. collaborators included Ellen Owen of the University of Washington and Jonathan E. Owen of Emory University. Potential Implications for US According to the Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service of the U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA), the Asian longhorned tick has been found across much of the eastern United States, from New York south to Georgia and west to Missouri. The invasive species can heavily infest livestock and poses a potential threat to animal and human health by transmitting pathogens. However, the USDA currently has no evidence that ALTNV is circulating in U.S. tick populations or causing human infections in the United States. Conversation 1 Comments Conversations are moderated.
